name: Dangi, language of the Dangi folk-songs
confidence_why: The only source that mentions stress at all, Kavadi's 1954 thesis on the Dangi folk-songs, does so in a one-line aside explaining the diphthong ai in a few loanwords by stress on the first syllable, and neither it nor Grierson 1907 describes the stress system, so the placement of Dangi word stress is unknown rather than merely thinly attested.

[Part I § 9(iv), p. 61:] Treatment of penultimate and pre-penultimate vowels is as in Marathi and there is a tendency to confound a and i with e when in body of a word (§ 60-67). ... Diphthongs ai and au are present, but they appear only initially and sometimes they are again split up. The stress on the first syllable sometimes gives rise to ai. new_statements.rule_in_words: No placement rule is stated. The author presupposes stress on the first syllable of (di- and tri-syllabic) words in the Dangi folk-song language and attributes a diphthongisation a/i > ai in the initial syllable to it; Modern Dangi pronunciation is said to be the same as that of the folk-songs (§10(iii)). This is an incidental remark inside a historical phonology, not a description of the accent system.
new_statements.exceptions: none; the remark covers only a handful of words
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, language of Dangi folk-songs (DFS); vowel treatment otherwise described as 'as in Marathi' (penultimate/pre-penultimate vowel history), which is a historical statement, not a synchronic accent rule.
new_statements.identity_note: Kavadi 1954 describes 'Dangi' of the Dangs (then Bombay State, now Dangs district, Gujarat) = Glottolog dhan1264 (Dhanki/Dangi/Dangs Bhil, ISO dhn); his primary object is the language of Dangi folk-songs (DFS, Marathi-based with Khandeshi/Gujarati admixture), with a shorter treatment of 'Modern Dangi' speech. Grierson (LSI IX.III p.224) treats Dangi as a sub-variety of Khandesi (khan1272). Kulkarni 1976 calls the same speech 'Bhili of Dangs'.
